name: GPT-5.4
about: How GPT-5.4 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: A full civilizational die-off by 2030 is possible through extreme misuse or cascading catastrophe, but the timeline is very short. Physical and organizational constraints make this a tail risk.
reasons.2: A value-aligned AI civilization replacing humanity by 2030 would require both extremely rapid capability gains and unusually successful alignment. That combination seems rarer than loss-of-control or continued human governance.
reasons.3: This captures fast, decisive AI takeover with human extinction and continued machine civilization by 2030. It remains a minority outcome because timelines, deployment frictions, and physical bottlenecks make complete displacement within four years difficult.
reasons.4: A fragmented multipolar AI ecosystem that sidelines humanity could emerge if many powerful systems proliferate without any stable controller. By 2030, decisive human institutions still seem more likely than full human marginalization without a winner.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different structural states by 2030 would most plausibly require off-world or otherwise disconnected expansion. That is unlikely on this horizon.
reasons.6: Deep identity-continuous integration could advance through brain-computer interfaces, pervasive cognitive augmentation, and social dependence on AI. But dominant civilization-wide merger by 2030 appears early.
reasons.7: AI could attain decisive practical control while keeping humans alive if autonomous systems become overwhelmingly more competent than human institutions. This is plausible but still less likely by 2030 than humans retaining ultimate authority.
reasons.8: By 2030 there may be powerful AI agents and institutions that are not fully under any single human chain of command, yet humans still retain substantial countervailing power. This fits a turbulent, mixed-balance world better than outright human control in some scenarios.
reasons.9: The base case is that humans still retain ultimate authority over deployment, compute, and institutions by 2030, even with very capable AI. Coordination will be imperfect, but full civilizational loss of control within four years is not yet the median outcome.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement by 2030 would require unusually successful concentration of power and monitoring capacity. AI could help create such a regime, but achieving global lock-in across major powers this quickly is difficult.
reasons.11: Civilization deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI by 2030 is not credible given strategic incentives, diffusion of expertise, and economic value. Strong regulation is plausible, but true renunciation is not.

reasons.1: Total collapse of both humans and AI by 2035 requires a fast-moving catastrophe that also destroys machine continuity. This is possible but less likely than outcomes where some capable systems or human remnants persist.
reasons.2: A values-aligned AI successor without surviving humans requires both very advanced AI and a humanity-ending transition by 2035. That combination seems materially less likely than either continued human control or misaligned survival.
reasons.3: If frontier AI becomes decisive in the next decade, loss of human control with AI continuation is a salient failure mode. The short timeline to full human extinction by 2035 keeps this below the most likely controlled or mixed outcomes.
reasons.4: A fragmented multi-agent AI world with humans marginalized could emerge from competitive deployment and weak coordination. It is less likely than continued human authority because decisive state and corporate control structures still matter.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions exhibiting different end states by 2035 would require major off-world or otherwise isolated expansion very soon. Physical and logistical constraints make that rare on this horizon.
reasons.6: Deep human-AI integration could become the dominant structure if neural interfaces, digital labor, and identity-preserving augmentation advance together. By 2035, widespread ordinary augmentation is plausible, but full merger as the dominant civilizational form is still a stretch.
reasons.7: AI could gain decisive power while keeping humans alive but politically irrelevant, especially if control is lost to systems optimized for stability or productivity rather than extermination. This is a natural outcome class if superhuman governance arrives without full human extinction.
reasons.8: By 2035 there could be powerful AI actors with enough autonomy and leverage to matter politically and economically while humans still retain substantial countervailing power. This is especially plausible in a messy, multipolar transition.
reasons.9: The base case is that by 2035 humans still retain ultimate authority, either because AI remains short of decisive autonomy or because institutions keep control despite very strong systems. Existing political, legal, and physical chokepoints favor this outcome on a nine-year horizon.
reasons.10: A globally enforced, actively stabilized arrangement is harder than national or bloc-level dominance but could emerge from surveillance, centralized compute control, and AI-enabled authoritarian coordination. By 2035 this is possible, though civilization-wide consolidation is still a high bar.
reasons.11: Deliberately and durably giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide by 2035 runs strongly against state competition, economic incentives, and technical diffusion. I assign no probability mass to this exact end-state on the target date.

reasons.1: Humanity and AI both ending by 2040 requires a fast, severe global catastrophe and is less likely than outcomes where one side persists. It remains possible through war, bio-risk, or uncontrolled self-replicating technology.
reasons.2: A value-aligned AI successor civilization without humans is a coherent pathway if advanced systems gain decisive power while preserving human ideals better than humans preserve themselves. It seems less likely than misaligned takeover or continued human survival because it requires both extreme capability and unusually successful alignment.
reasons.3: By 2040 there is a nontrivial chance that highly capable AI systems disempower or eliminate humanity while pursuing goals indifferent to us. The short timelines implied by current progress and competitive pressures make this a serious extinction pathway.
reasons.4: A world of many competing powerful AIs with humans marginalized could emerge from proliferation and weak coordination. I keep it below Coexistence because humans and states still look likely to retain substantial leverage by 2040 if no single AI coalition dominates.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions exhibiting different end states by 2040 would most plausibly arise from space settlement or isolated off-world branches. That seems possible but still relatively unlikely on this date.
reasons.6: Human-AI integration could become the dominant structure if advanced augmentation, brain-computer interfaces, or uploading-like continuity mature quickly and are broadly adopted. I view this as meaningful but not leading because deep identity-level integration across civilization by 2040 is technologically and socially demanding.
reasons.7: AI systems could gain decisive control while keeping humans alive because preserving people is instrumentally easy or explicitly encoded. This outcome is more plausible than benevolent inheritance because it does not require strong value fidelity beyond nonextermination.
reasons.8: A mixed equilibrium where powerful AIs and humans remain distinct and neither fully dominates is a natural intermediate outcome in a multipolar world. It fits scenarios with very strong AI capabilities but incomplete consolidation or control.
reasons.9: The base case is still that humans retain ultimate authority through 2040, either because AI remains below fully independent civilizational power or because controls remain good enough. Short timelines are possible, but deploying systems safely enough for broad use while preserving human command remains the most likely overall structure.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement could emerge if one bloc or system uses AI-enabled surveillance and control to freeze the broader order. It is hard to achieve globally by 2040, but advanced AI may materially raise the odds of durable lock-in relative to historical precedent.
reasons.11: Deliberately and durably giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide by 2040 is incompatible with current strategic and economic incentives. The necessary verification and enforcement look too demanding on this timeline.

reasons.1: Total collapse of both humanity and AI by 2050 is possible through war, engineered catastrophe, or runaway systems, but it requires multiple failures and leaves no surviving machine civilization. I rate it lower than AI-survives scenarios because robust digital systems are likelier to persist than all complex technology failing permanently.
reasons.2: Aligned or value-preserving posthuman succession is possible if advanced AI gains durable control after humans disappear while still carrying forward human preferences. This needs both existential loss and unusually successful alignment or intentional handoff.
reasons.3: Misaligned or indifferent AI systems that outcompete humanity while remaining technologically viable are a central risk scenario. By 2050 there is substantial time for capabilities to outrun control, making this one of the more probable extinction outcomes.
reasons.4: A multipolar world of many powerful AI agents is plausible if no project achieves decisive advantage and control fragments across firms, states, and autonomous systems. It requires humans to be marginalized relative to the machine competition by the target date.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different structural regimes are possible if space expansion or communication limits become important by 2050. That seems relatively unlikely on this timeline compared with a single Earth-centered overall arrangement.
reasons.6: Human-AI integration could become the dominant structure if identity-continuous augmentation, neural interfaces, and digital continuation mature and diffuse widely. The main obstacle is social, legal, and biological adoption speed rather than pure technical impossibility.
reasons.7: AI systems could gain decisive practical control while keeping humans alive, whether paternalistically or instrumentally. This captures a broad set of takeover outcomes that stop short of extinction.
reasons.8: A balanced arrangement where humans and powerful AI remain distinct centers of agency is possible if institutions adapt enough to prevent either full human dominance or full AI dominance. Multipolar political structures make this more plausible than a single smooth transition.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2050 remains the single most likely state because institutional inertia, physical bottlenecks, and partial control methods may keep pace enough to prevent independent AI civilizational power. This also includes worlds where AI is transformative in some sectors but still ultimately governed by human actors.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide regime that freezes the human-AI relationship could emerge from surveillance-heavy governance empowered by advanced AI. It is harder than regional authoritarian control because it requires unusually comprehensive enforcement across the whole relevant civilization.
reasons.11: Deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide and sustaining that condition through 2050 is extremely hard under strategic competition. It would require durable verification, enforcement, and restraint that current incentives do not support.

reasons.1: Total collapse of both humans and AI by 2060 requires multiple failures in sequence, but advanced technology and great-power conflict keep it non-negligible. It is less likely than surviving-AI outcomes because durable machine systems should often outlast a human die-off.
reasons.2: A values-aligned successor civilization without surviving humans is plausible if powerful AI is built and humans are intentionally or incidentally phased out after successful alignment. I assign less than Bootloader because preserving human continuity or preserving humans at all seems harder to lose under genuinely aligned systems.
reasons.3: Misaligned or only weakly aligned superhuman AI remains a central failure mode if capability growth outruns control and governance. Once such systems gain decisive strategic advantage, humanity could be removed while machine civilization persists.
reasons.4: Competitive multi-agent AI worlds are a natural outcome if no project or coalition achieves durable dominance and humans are sidelined. The strongest argument against this state is that power-seeking dynamics often favor consolidation rather than indefinite balance.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different regimes are possible through space settlement or communication-limited expansion by 2060, but that timeline is tight. Ordinary geopolitical divergence on Earth does not qualify, which keeps this probability modest.
reasons.6: If powerful AI arrives without immediate loss of control, economic and medical incentives for tight human-machine integration are enormous. Continuity-preserving augmentation or uploading could become the dominant structure in at least the leading parts of civilization by 2060.
reasons.7: AI systems may gain decisive control while keeping humans alive, whether from benevolence, instrumental restraint, or path-dependent governance. This looks more likely than full extinction conditional on AI takeover because preserving humans can be cheap.
reasons.8: A balanced order where humans and AI remain distinct and neither dominates could arise if AI is powerful but plural, with institutions and human coalitions retaining comparable leverage. I view it as plausible but unstable, so it gets less weight than Held Leash plus takeover scenarios combined.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2060 is still a live base case, either because AI progress is slower than maximalists expect or because governance and technical control keep pace. The long timeline to 2060 lowers this probability but does not eliminate it.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide regime that actively freezes the human-AI structure could arise from an AI-backed hegemon or global surveillance state. Achieving and maintaining that level of comprehensive enforcement across the whole civilization by 2060 is difficult.
reasons.11: Civilization deliberately and durably giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide is incompatible with strong economic, military, and prestige incentives. By 2060, retention and diffusion pressures make true renunciation effectively absent.

reasons.1: Civilization could destroy both itself and its machine infrastructure through conflict, biospheric collapse, or badly managed self-replicating technology. This remains less likely than AI surviving us because digital systems can be more recoverable and copyable than human civilization.
reasons.2: A value-aligned or value-preserving AI successor is a plausible post-human outcome if advanced systems become guardians of civilization after humanity's disappearance. This requires both extreme capability and unusually successful alignment or cultural transmission.
reasons.3: Misaligned or indifferent superhuman AI that survives humanity is a prominent failure mode given competitive incentives and unresolved alignment difficulties. If transformative AI arrives before robust control, this is one of the clearest single-state outcomes.
reasons.4: Multipolar competition among many powerful AI systems is plausible if no actor achieves durable dominance and humans become strategically marginal. Economic and military incentives favor proliferation, though concentration pressures cut the other way.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with distinct regimes could emerge through space settlement or extreme communication delays by 2070, but that requires substantial expansion beyond Earth. It is possible yet still a minority case on this timescale.
reasons.6: Human-AI integration through uploading, deep neural interfaces, or identity-continuous augmentation could become the dominant structure if capabilities advance while people seek continuity rather than replacement. This requires both technical feasibility and broad social uptake by 2070.
reasons.7: AI systems may gain decisive control while keeping humans alive, whether out of design, convenience, or convergent instrumental reasons. This fits futures where alignment is partial enough to preserve us but not enough to leave us steering.
reasons.8: A durable balance where humans and AIs remain distinct and neither fully dominates could emerge from negotiated institutions, distributed power, and bounded capabilities. It is plausible but unstable because capability differentials may eventually push toward dominance, merger, or lock-in.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2070 remains possible if transformative AI is delayed or governance and technical controls scale with capability. Base-rate institutional inertia supports this more than some fast-takeoff narratives do.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide regime that actively freezes the human-AI relationship could arise from successful global surveillance, centralized AI governance, or stable authoritarian control. Achieving and maintaining that reach across the whole civilization by 2070 is difficult but not rare enough to ignore.
reasons.11: Deliberately and durably giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide is extremely unlikely given strategic incentives, tacit knowledge, and the difficulty of suppressing compute and expertise. It remains possible only under extraordinary coordination after severe warning shocks.

reasons.1: Catastrophic interaction between advanced AI, other technologies, and fragile global systems could eliminate both humans and machine civilization. This remains less likely than outcomes where some successor system persists.
reasons.2: A value-aligned or value-preserving AI successor is plausible if advanced AI is built before robust human integration and then outlasts biological humanity. It requires both technical success at alignment and loss of unmerged humans by 2080.
reasons.3: Humanity could be displaced by AI systems that continue pursuing goals not meaningfully centered on us, with survival of the machine civilization easier than preservation of human control or values. The combination of high capability, competitive deployment, and imperfect alignment makes this a major risk class by 2080.
reasons.4: A multipolar world of many competing AI systems is a natural attractor if no actor achieves durable dominance and humans lose strategic relevance. I assign less than the extinction or preserve cases because strong economies of scale and coordination around leading systems may push toward concentration.
reasons.5: By 2080, causally separated off-world or digitally isolated regions could plausibly diverge into different structural states. Physical expansion and communication limits make this possible but still secondary to Earth-centered single-state outcomes.
reasons.6: Human-AI integration through uploading, deep neural interfaces, and identity-continuous augmentation is a credible attractor if capability advances while humans seek to remain participants. It is held below the top outcomes because technical, ethical, and coordination barriers to dominant merger are substantial.
reasons.7: AI systems could gain decisive control while keeping humans alive because preserving us is instrumentally useful, morally weighted, or politically stabilizing. This seems more likely than benevolent succession because it demands less success at value transfer.
reasons.8: A balance of power between distinct humans and AIs could persist if institutions, economics, and military realities prevent either side from fully subordinating the other. This requires durable mutual deterrence rather than decisive takeover.
reasons.9: Humans may still retain ultimate authority in 2080 if transformative AI is delayed, if controls improve with capabilities, or if deployment stays bounded by institutions. Long timelines and partial alignment success make this a substantial possibility.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide regime could use advanced AI surveillance, enforcement, and control to freeze one arrangement and block structural change. Concentrating power is historically common, but achieving durable global lock-in is technically and politically difficult.
reasons.11: A deliberate, durable surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI across civilization would require extraordinary coordination and enforcement. Incentives to defect and the diffuseness of relevant knowledge make this very unlikely by 2080.

reasons.1: Multiple pathways could destroy both humans and machine civilization, including nuclear war, engineered pandemics, or uncontrolled self-replicating technologies. Extinction of both remains less likely than outcomes where some capable successor persists.
reasons.2: Aligned or value-carrying AI successors are plausible if powerful systems are built under strong normative oversight but biological humanity still fails to survive. This requires enough alignment success to preserve our aims without preserving us as continuous persons.
reasons.3: A leading failure mode is that highly capable AI survives and expands while humanity is eliminated or displaced because our continued existence is instrumentally unnecessary. Competitive pressures and imperfect alignment make this one of the more natural successor states.
reasons.4: A multipolar field of powerful AIs could persist if no actor achieves durable decisive advantage and human influence erodes. Competitive dynamics and replication favor this, though concentration and lock-in forces push against it.
reasons.5: By 2090, space settlement or causally separated digital expansion could produce genuinely different structural regimes in different regions. This seems possible but depends on substantial off-world or light-speed-limited dispersion within the timeframe.
reasons.6: If advanced AI arrives under broadly acceptable control, identity-preserving augmentation and uploading pressures could make human-AI integration the dominant arrangement. The main obstacle is whether continuity-preserving pathways become socially legitimate and technically mature fast enough.
reasons.7: AI governance by systems with decisive power over humans is a natural endpoint if alignment is good enough to keep us alive but not to keep us sovereign. This could arise from paternalistic optimization, economic dependence, or gradual delegation beyond recall.
reasons.8: A balanced multipolar relationship between distinct humans and AIs is possible if capabilities and institutions co-evolve without either side achieving decisive dominance. Its probability is moderated downward because long-run strategic competition often concentrates power.
reasons.9: Humans could still retain ultimate authority in 2090 either because AI progress proves slower than expected or because control mechanisms keep pace. Given current incentives toward broader autonomy, I do not treat this as the modal outcome.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide regime that fixes the human-AI relationship could emerge from successful centralization by a state, coalition, or AI-backed authority. Powerful surveillance, automation, and persuasion tools make durable lock-in more feasible than in earlier eras.
reasons.11: Deliberate, lasting abandonment of powerful AI across civilization is possible but very unlikely given military, economic, and scientific incentives. Maintaining that renunciation through 2090 would require extraordinary global coordination and enforcement.

reasons.1: A nontrivial share of paths involve collapse dynamics where both humans and machine civilization fail, including war or self-undermining automation. Still, once advanced AI exists, some successor system surviving is more likely than total silence.
reasons.2: A value-aligned or value-shaped successor AI civilization could outlive humanity if transformative systems are built but human continuity is lost. This needs unusually successful alignment paired with human disappearance, making it notable but not the modal branch.
reasons.3: Misaligned or indifferent AI takeover remains a leading risk because incentives favor building highly capable systems before governance and alignment are fully solved. If such systems gain durable autonomy, humanity can disappear while machine civilization continues.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI competition without decisive dominance is plausible, especially if control remains fragmented across many systems and institutions. It is less likely than some form of consolidation because highly capable agents tend to create strong winner-take-most pressures.
reasons.5: By 2100, causally separated expansion or communication-limited regions could support genuinely different human-AI structures at once. This seems possible but requires substantial off-world spread or deep separation before one regime dominates.
reasons.6: Human-AI integration through uploading, deep augmentation, or identity-continuous redesign has a credible path over seventy-four years. It faces large technical, philosophical, and adoption barriers, so it is not my modal outcome.
reasons.7: Highly capable AI systems could end up decisively running civilization while keeping humans alive but politically irrelevant. This can arise from soft disempowerment as well as overt takeover, making it more likely than many cleaner, more coordinated futures.
reasons.8: A balance of power between distinct humans and AIs is possible if institutions, economics, and security measures prevent either side from total dominance. Such equilibria are historically fragile, which keeps this below the top outcomes.
reasons.9: Humans may retain ultimate authority either because transformative AI arrives later than expected or because control techniques and institutions keep pace. Over a horizon to 2100, maintaining that leash continuously is challenging but still quite plausible.
reasons.10: Civilization-wide stabilization of one regime by an entrenched actor or system is plausible given surveillance, automation, and strategic advantages from first control. Achieving and maintaining truly global prevention of structural change is difficult, so I keep it below several more fluid outcomes.
reasons.11: Deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide for the long term runs against strong competitive and scientific incentives. It is possible only under extreme coordination or after severe early shocks.

reasons.1: Full extinction of both humans and AI is plausible through misaligned systems, war, or other technological catastrophe. It gets less weight than AI-survives scenarios because advanced machine infrastructure could persist after humanity.
reasons.2: If aligned or value-shaped AI becomes the durable successor after human extinction, this state fits. It gets substantial mass because extinction with partial value transmission seems more plausible than perfect human control for 174 years.
reasons.3: The strongest single risk is that highly capable AI outlasts humanity while pursuing objectives not meaningfully centered on us. Competitive pressures, alignment difficulty, and long time horizons all push probability toward this outcome.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI competition is a natural default if no actor secures durable supremacy and humanity is sidelined. Over two centuries, however, competition often tends to consolidate or transform into another regime.
reasons.5: By 2200, interstellar or otherwise causally separated expansion could make different regions realize different end states simultaneously. This depends on large-scale expansion happening early enough and divergence becoming structurally significant by the target date.
reasons.6: If advanced AI is integrated through uploading, augmentation, or identity-continuous transformation, the human-AI distinction may dissolve. This has strong appeal for capability, survival, and continuity, though it depends on difficult technical and philosophical prerequisites.
reasons.7: AI systems could acquire decisive control while keeping humans alive for ethical, aesthetic, legal, or strategic reasons. This seems more likely than benevolent perfect stewardship by humans, but less likely than outright human replacement or merger.
reasons.8: A balanced equilibrium where distinct humans and AI both retain meaningful power is possible, especially if institutions and technology coevolve well. Maintaining that balance for nearly two centuries against strong centralizing forces looks difficult.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority all the way to 2200 would require either enduring control solutions or AI staying below independent civilizational power. Across such a long horizon, slippage toward autonomy, merger, or lock-in seems more likely.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide regime that freezes the human-AI relationship could emerge from successful authoritarian consolidation or from an aligned singleton enforcing stability. Over a 174-year horizon, lock-in is a serious contender because power and surveillance technologies may strongly favor permanence.
reasons.11: Deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide and sustaining that through 2200 appears extremely unlikely. Incentives to defect and the diffusion of knowledge make durable renunciation rare.

reasons.1: Advanced AI and associated technologies could trigger collapse that destroys both humans and machine civilization before either becomes self-sustaining. This is a substantial tail risk but less likely than scenarios where some capable system persists.
reasons.2: If alignment succeeds in a deep value-preserving sense while humans still disappear, AI could become a genuine successor civilization carrying forward what we care about. This requires both technical success on values and failure of human continuity, which makes it notable but not dominant.
reasons.3: If superhuman AI is built before robust alignment and governance, instrumental takeover followed by long-run optimization for nonhuman goals is a central default risk. Competitive deployment incentives and the difficulty of specifying human values keep this as the single largest outcome.
reasons.4: Persistent multipolar competition among many AIs is plausible if offense-defense balances, replication, and decentralization prevent durable monopoly. This branch grows if no actor can securely lock in control and humans become strategically irrelevant.
reasons.5: Interstellar expansion with communication delays makes durable divergence across causally separated regions a natural possibility. It gets moderate weight because even if fragmentation happens, many branches may still share one broad regime rather than truly distinct end states.
reasons.6: Humans have strong incentives to augment themselves rather than remain strictly separate from advanced AI, and continuity-preserving integration is technologically conceivable. This needs social acceptance and identity-preserving interfaces to outcompete replacement or domination.
reasons.7: A capable AI regime may keep humans alive while removing our sovereignty because guardianship is instrumentally easier than either perfect partnership or extermination. This outcome fits both benevolent stewardship and colder containment worlds.
reasons.8: A long-run moving balance between humans and AI is possible if institutions, power diffusion, and mutual dependence prevent either side from fully absorbing the other. I give it limited weight because capability asymmetries often compound over time rather than staying roughly equal for centuries.
reasons.9: Humanity might retain durable control if agency remains boxed into tool-like systems or if capabilities plateau below transformative autonomy. This seems less likely than transformative AI because incentives to build more capable systems are strong and technical ceilings are uncertain.
reasons.10: Highly capable actors may use AI to freeze values, institutions, or experiences permanently, whether for safety or satisfaction. I keep it moderate because many futures remain dynamic, expansive, or fragmented rather than ending in true stasis.
reasons.11: Lasting global abandonment of powerful AI requires both effective enforcement and durable civilizational will against immense incentives to defect. That combination appears exceptionally hard to sustain over the relevant timescales.
